notes.b: The investigation is an individual study of a geographical question, carried out under the teacher's supervision and written up in the SEC report booklet. It is worth 20% of the total mark.
points: It is compulsory at Higher and Ordinary level, and is assessed outside the written examination, so it does not appear as a question on the written paper.
The topic is chosen from the prescribed list that the State Examinations Commission (SEC) issues for each year's examination.

Typical topic areas are physical (rivers, coasts, glacial or karst landscapes, weather, soils, rocks) and human (urban land use, traffic, settlement, economic activity), but only the year's own list applies.
The SEC sets the completion date each year: for 2027 the completed report goes to the teacher by 16 April 2027, and the school then submits it to the SEC.
A class may work on one investigation and collect data together, but each student must write a full and complete report of their own. Group reports are not accepted.

Primary sources (first-hand fieldwork data) must make up at least 60% of the information gathered, and every source must be referenced, including any material generated using AI; unreferenced material counts as plagiarism.
The report is authenticated by the candidate and by the teacher; copying from classmates, textbooks or websites, other than essential references such as definitions, makes the report invalid.

The report is completed in the official SEC Reporting Booklet, which has been completed and submitted digitally since the 2025 examination; the typed text is no more than 1,000 words, and examiners mark only what is in the booklet.

notes.h: The booklet's marks and word limits
notes.b: The booklet divides the report into five stages, each with its own marks. Stages 1 to 4 also have word limits that add up to 1,000 words.
points: Stage 1, Introduction: 5 marks, no more than 50 words.
Stage 2, Planning: 5 marks, no more than 100 words.
Stage 3, Gathering of information: 40 marks, no more than 450 words.
Stage 4, Results, conclusions and evaluation: 30 marks, no more than 400 words.
Stage 5, Presentation of results: 20 marks, for hand-drawn graphs and diagrams added to the booklet's image pages.
The marks are the same at Higher and Ordinary level, but Higher Level answers are expected to develop each heading fully, with detailed analysis and comparison with theory.

notes.b: The introduction states a hypothesis to test or the aims of the study, in no more than 50 words.
points: Hypothesis: a precise, testable statement that the data can prove or disprove, e.g. a measurable claim about change with distance downstream.
Aim: a statement of what the investigation sets out to find out. Use a hypothesis or an aim, as the booklet asks.
A hypothesis is a testable statement, not a question or a topic title.
Fifty words is room for one hypothesis or two or three short aims, so leave the detail of tasks and methods to Stage 2.
Write the statement so that Stage 4 can say it is accepted, rejected or partly accepted, and so every later stage traces back to it.
Good practice: keep the hypothesis narrow enough to test in a day or two of fieldwork, avoid vague words such as "better" or "nice", and include the place studied.
Illustrative hypothesis for a river study of the River Dallow upstream of Rivertown: "The velocity of the River Dallow increases downstream."

notes.b: Planning identifies the information required and the methods or tasks for gathering it, in no more than 100 words, and distinguishes primary from secondary sources.
points: Types of information required: primary (measurements, observations, counts, questionnaire answers) and secondary (maps, statistics, texts), with a note of how each secondary source will be accessed.
Objectives: specific, measurable tasks that together test the hypothesis, each naming what will be measured and where.

Illustrative tasks for the River Dallow: measure channel width, average depth and velocity at five sites 500 m apart; calculate cross-sectional area and discharge at each site; measure the size of ten pebbles at each site.
Illustrative information required: primary measurements, and a secondary OS map and aerial photograph of the river.

Within 100 words the stage names the methods, says why each suits the hypothesis, and mentions the design of the recording sheet or questionnaire; the fuller preparation below is done but not all written up.
Before fieldwork, study OS maps and aerial photographs of the area.
Choose and justify sites: e.g. evenly spaced along a river, or sample points across a town.
Choose the date and time, gather the equipment, divide tasks within the group and arrange landowner permission where needed.
Recording sheet: a table prepared in advance, with columns for site, time, each measurement and repeat readings, so that data are recorded consistently.
Questionnaire design: keep it short, with closed questions (tick boxes, yes/no, rating scales) for easy analysis and a few open questions.
Questionnaire wording must be neutral and unbiased, with no unnecessary personal questions; pilot it with a few people first.
Sampling plan for a questionnaire: who is asked, where, when and how many.

Safety and ethics: complete a risk assessment, never work alone, supervise near water or traffic, wear suitable clothing and footwear, check the weather and river level, and respect property and the environment.
Questionnaires are anonymous and voluntary.
Good practice: explain why each method suits its objective, and describe the method clearly enough for someone else to repeat it.

Illustrative planning for the River Dallow: sites on the OS map where the river is accessible and safe; a recording sheet with columns for site, width, depths at five points, three float times over 10 m and pebble lengths; a risk assessment of low river level, wellingtons and groups of four.

notes.b: The gathering stage describes the tasks or methods used, the equipment and how information was recorded, in no more than 450 words. It carries 40 marks, the most of any stage.
points: The examiner's marking boxes cover two methods plus coherence, so two methods described fully earn more than many described thinly.
Each method says what was done, where, with which equipment, how results were recorded, and how many sites, readings or responses were taken, so that someone else could repeat it.
Measuring tape or ranging poles: channel width, beach width and distances.
Metre stick: depth at regular intervals across a channel.
Float and stopwatch, or a flow meter: velocity. Time a float over a measured distance, repeat the timing and average the results.
Clinometer: the slope angle of a beach or valley side.
Callipers or a ruler measure pebble size; a roundness chart measures pebble shape.
Compass: orientation, aspect and wind direction.
Weather instruments: thermometer, rain gauge, anemometer and wind vane.
Camera: a photographic record, dated and located.
GPS or a smartphone mapping app: locating sites.
Field observations: labelled field sketches, land-use mapping on a base map, traffic or pedestrian counts at set times, and environmental quality surveys using scored criteria.

notes.h: Secondary sources and accuracy in collection
points: Secondary sources used in investigations include OS maps and aerial photographs, census data, weather records, local authority plans, textbooks and websites; the notes on Textual sources explains how to evaluate them.
Record full details of each secondary source when you collect it, for acknowledgement.
Take repeat readings and average them.
Use the same method and the same people at every site.
Record units, and note the conditions: weather, time and river level.

Problems to name in the report: bad weather or high water that makes measurement unsafe, equipment faults, a float caught in vegetation, people refusing questionnaires, restricted access to a site, and time limits.
For each problem, state the problem, its effect on the data and the solution.
Illustrative: at site 3 the float snagged on reeds twice; the group discarded those runs and took three clean timings.

notes.b: Illustrative values from the River Dallow study show the calculations used in the results.
points: Velocity = distance ÷ time, using the average of the repeated float timings.
Cross-sectional area = width × average depth (m²).
Discharge = cross-sectional area × velocity (m³ per second).
Illustrative site 1: width 3.0 m; average depth 0.20 m; average float time over 10 m of 25 s, so velocity 0.4 m/s; cross-sectional area 0.6 m²; discharge 0.24 m³/s.
Illustrative site 5: width 6.0 m; average depth 0.40 m; average float time over 10 m of 10 s, so velocity 1.0 m/s; cross-sectional area 2.4 m²; discharge 2.4 m³/s.

notes.b: Stage 4 covers results, conclusions and evaluation together, in no more than 400 words, for 30 marks. Results come first and state what the data show, with figures.
points: State each finding in words with its key figures, and refer to the graph or table that shows it.
Higher Level statistical analysis: averages (mean and median), range and percentages.
Results can be calculated with a calculator or spreadsheet, but no software may be used to create the graphs, charts, tables, maps or diagrams in the booklet.
Describe trends with figures, e.g. "velocity rose from site 1 to site 5", note anomalies and suggest their causes.
Keep results separate from conclusions.

notes.b: The conclusion tests the hypothesis against the results, explains the pattern and compares the findings with established theory.
points: State whether the hypothesis is accepted, rejected or partly accepted, using the evidence from each objective.
Explain the findings geographically: say why the pattern occurs.
Bradshaw model: downstream, a river's discharge, channel width, depth and velocity tend to increase, while gradient and load particle size decrease.
Burgess concentric zone model (Chicago, 1925): describes urban land use in zones around a central business district.
Compare results with the textbook model or published work, and explain any differences, such as local geology, human interference or a small sample.

Illustrative conclusion: the hypothesis is accepted because velocity rose from 0.4 m/s to 1.0 m/s; this matches the Bradshaw model, which is explained by greater depth reducing friction and more water from tributaries.

notes.b: The evaluation judges how reliable the data are, names the limits of the study and proposes specific improvements.
points: Evaluate the reliability and accuracy of the data, and say what went well.
Name the limits of the study: one day's data, few sites, a small questionnaire sample, measurement error and the weather on the day.
A surface float overestimates average velocity, so float results are estimates, not exact values.
Improvements: more sites, repeat visits in different seasons or conditions, better equipment such as a flow meter, larger samples and a longer stretch of river.
Suggest further investigation that the findings point towards.
Skills gained (optional): teamwork, fieldwork skills, ICT and report writing, which the syllabus links to working conditions similar to those likely to be encountered in the world of work.

notes.b: Results are presented in graphic form on the booklet's image pages and discussed in Stage 4. Presentation is marked out of 20.
points: Illustrations include tables of raw and averaged data, sketch maps locating sites, annotated photographs and field sketches.
The examiner's boxes cover two presentation methods plus coherence, so results are shown in at least two clearly different graphic forms.

Choose the graph that suits the data: a line graph for change with distance or time, a bar chart for comparison between sites, a pie chart for shares, a scatter graph for a relationship, and channel cross-sections for showing a river channel's shape.
Every illustration is titled, labelled, has units and a key, and is referred to in the text. Graph-drawing technique is in the notes on Figure interpretation.
Every sketch, map, diagram, graph, chart and table is the student's own hand-drawn work, inserted into the digital booklet as an image such as a photo or scan.
Illustrations go only on the booklet's image pages, because examiners mark only what is in the booklet.
For the River Dallow study, the illustrations are: a line graph of velocity against distance downstream; channel cross-sections drawn to scale for sites 1 and 5; and a sketch map of the five sites.
Within each stage, marks are awarded for significant relevant points (SRPs), and Stage 5 is marked on the graphic illustrations.
Marks are earned by a clear, testable hypothesis or aim within the word limit.
Marks are earned by methods described step by step, with equipment named and justified.
Marks are earned by accurate data presented in varied, well-labelled illustrations, and by results that refer to the actual figures.
Marks are earned by conclusions that answer the hypothesis and are supported by the results, comparison with theory, and an honest evaluation with specific improvements.
Marks are lost for vague or untestable hypotheses, methods listed without explanation, and results given without figures.
Marks are lost for generic evaluations such as "it went well", for writing outside the space provided, and for material copied from others or the internet.

keyTerms.definition: A precise, testable statement that the data can prove or disprove.
A specific, measurable task that tests part of the hypothesis and receives its own results.
A table prepared in advance, with columns for each site, time, measurement and repeat reading.
Estimating velocity by timing a float over a measured distance, repeating the timing and averaging the results.
The area of a river channel's cross-section, calculated as width × average depth.
The volume of water passing a point each second, calculated as cross-sectional area × velocity, in m³ per second.
A distinct, relevant fact or explanation that earns a mark in a section of the report.
A model of how a river's discharge, width, depth and velocity tend to change downstream.

factCards.term: Geographical Investigation: weighting, topic list and deadline
factCards.definition: Worth 20% of the total mark (written exam 80%) and compulsory at Higher and Ordinary level. The topic comes from the SEC's prescribed list for that year; the completed report goes to the teacher by 16 April 2027 for the 2027 examination.

factCards.term: Geographical Investigation: rules on group work, sources and authenticity
factCards.definition: A class may collect data together, but each student writes a full report of their own; group reports are not accepted. At least 60% of the information must come from primary sources. The report is authenticated by the candidate and the teacher.

factCards.term: Investigation hypothesis: the rules, with an illustrative example
factCards.definition: A precise, testable statement, not a question or topic title; narrow enough to test in a day or two; no vague words such as 'better'; the place named. Illustrative: 'The velocity of the River Dallow increases downstream.'

factCards.term: Geographical Investigation: marks and word limits by stage
factCards.definition: Introduction 5 marks (50 words), Planning 5 (100 words), Gathering of information 40 (450 words), Results, conclusions and evaluation 30 (400 words), Presentation of results 20; 1,000 words in total.

factCards.term: Investigation planning: tasks to complete before fieldwork
factCards.definition: Study OS maps and aerial photographs; choose and justify sites (e.g. evenly spaced along a river); choose the date and time; gather equipment; divide tasks in the group; arrange landowner permission; prepare a recording sheet with columns for repeat readings.

factCards.term: Questionnaire design for an investigation: the rules
factCards.definition: Keep it short; mostly closed questions (tick boxes, yes/no, rating scales) for easy analysis, plus a few open ones; neutral, unbiased wording; no unnecessary personal questions; pilot it first; plan who, where, when and how many to ask.

factCards.term: Fieldwork safety and ethics: precautions to state
factCards.definition: Complete a risk assessment; never work alone; supervision near water or traffic; suitable clothing and footwear; check the weather and river level; respect property and the environment; questionnaires anonymous and voluntary.

factCards.term: River study instruments: what each one measures
factCards.definition: Measuring tape or ranging poles: channel width; metre stick: depth at regular intervals across the channel; float and stopwatch, or a flow meter: velocity; clinometer: slope angle; callipers or ruler: pebble size; roundness chart: pebble shape.

factCards.term: Measuring velocity with a float: the method and its limitation
factCards.definition: Time a float over a measured distance, such as 10 m, repeat the timing and average it; velocity = distance ÷ time. A surface float overestimates average velocity, so the results are estimates, not exact values.

factCards.term: Discharge calculation: an illustrative worked example
factCards.definition: Illustrative site 5: width 6.0 m × average depth 0.40 m = cross-sectional area 2.4 m²; a float takes 10 s over 10 m, so velocity is 1.0 m/s; discharge = 2.4 × 1.0 = 2.4 m³/s.

factCards.term: Accuracy in data collection: four good practices
factCards.definition: Take repeat readings and average them; use the same method and the same people at every site; record the units; note the conditions, such as the weather, time and river level.

factCards.term: Problems encountered: what the report must say, with an example
factCards.definition: For each problem, state the problem, its effect on the data and the solution. Illustrative: at site 3 the float snagged on reeds twice, so those runs were discarded and three clean timings taken.

factCards.term: Investigation results: how to present each finding
factCards.definition: State each finding in words with its key figures and refer to the graph or table that shows it; describe trends with figures; note anomalies; keep results separate from conclusions. The graphs themselves go in Stage 5, in at least two different forms.

factCards.term: Investigation conclusion: three things it must do
factCards.definition: State whether the hypothesis is accepted, rejected or partly accepted, using each objective's evidence; explain the pattern geographically; compare with established theory (Bradshaw model for rivers, Burgess for urban land use) and explain differences.
Downstream, a river's discharge, channel width, depth and velocity tend to increase, while gradient and load particle size decrease.

factCards.term: Investigation evaluation: limitations and improvements to give
factCards.definition: Limits: one day's data, few sites, a small sample, measurement error, the weather on the day, a float measuring surface velocity only. Improvements: more sites, repeat visits in other seasons, a flow meter, larger samples, a longer stretch of river.

Vague or untestable hypotheses; going over a stage's word limit; methods listed without explanation; results without figures; unlabelled or irrelevant illustrations; conclusions not linked to results; generic evaluations ('it went well'); writing outside the booklet's space; copied material.

questions.prompt: State a hypothesis for an investigation of a river, and outline the information you would need to test it.
questions.model: Illustrative answer. Hypothesis: The velocity of the River Dallow increases downstream. Information required: primary measurements of channel width, average depth and velocity at five sites 500 m apart, used to calculate cross-sectional area and discharge at each site, and the size of ten pebbles at each site; secondary information from an OS map and aerial photograph of the river to locate safe, evenly spaced sites.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would measure the velocity and discharge of a river, and name one problem you might encounter and how you would overcome it.
questions.model: Illustrative answer. Velocity by the float method: mark a measured distance of 10 m along a straight stretch, release a float upstream, time it over the distance with a stopwatch, repeat three times and average the timings, then calculate velocity = distance ÷ time. Discharge: measure the channel width and average depth to find the cross-sectional area (width × average depth), then multiply by the velocity. Check with site 5: width 6.0 m × average depth 0.40 m = 2.4 m²; 2.4 m² × 1.0 m/s = 2.4 m³/s. Problem: the float snagged on reeds, so discard those runs and take three clean timings.

questions.prompt: Write a conclusion and evaluation for the River Dallow investigation using the results given.
questions.model: Illustrative answer. The hypothesis is accepted: velocity rose from 0.4 m/s at site 1 to 1.0 m/s at site 5. This matches the Bradshaw model, explained by greater depth reducing friction and more water from tributaries. Limitations: the data come from one day after dry weather; and a surface float overestimates average velocity. Improvements: use a flow meter, add more sites, and repeat visits after rain.
